solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Suffer, with quite pained expression

blocks.note: quite in the sense of entirely, all the way
the cry someone gives when hurt

explanation.surface: Someone endures their suffering while wearing a fairly pained look.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suffer' here is the old sense found in 'suffer the little children', not the sense of feeling pain.
explanation.definitionFit: In older English, to suffer something is to permit or tolerate it, a synonym for letting it happen.

clue.text: Fan of a fine old company performing song and dance

blocks.note: taken as written
F is the pencil-grade abbreviation for fine
Imperial Chemical Industries, a former British industrial giant
a performer is on, on stage
a song and dance is a fuss

explanation.surface: A devotee of some fine old theatrical troupe staging musical numbers.
explanation.walkthrough: ICI was Imperial Chemical Industries, a British chemicals firm broken up in 2008, hence 'old'; 'song and dance' means a fuss, not a show.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words name an enthusiastic devotee of some pursuit, such as bullfighting or opera; they are close synonyms.

clue.text: Many failing to finish: a policeman’s not happy?

definitions.note: an allusion standing for the noun

indicators.note: a word that does not finish loses its final letter

blocks.note: many; its final letter is then dropped

explanation.surface: A gloomy constable laments that most people never finish the job.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition quotes Gilbert and Sullivan's Pirates of Penzance: 'A policeman's lot is not a happy one.'
explanation.definitionFit: The famous song line describes a constable's fate or portion as unhappy, and that fate is what the clue asks for.

clue.text: Jan’s in this women’s team in Italy

blocks.note: W is the standard abbreviation for women
Inter Milan, the Italian football club

explanation.surface: A woman named Jan plays for a women's side in Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: Jan looks like a woman's name but is the abbreviation for January.
explanation.definitionFit: January falls in the coldest season in the northern hemisphere, so the month sits inside it.

clue.text: Briefly had success — they are about to retire

indicators.note: said briefly, a word is cut short by its final letter
to be about something is to surround it on every side

blocks.note: a hit is a success
taken as written; it goes around the shortened word
the word with its last letter dropped

explanation.surface: A brief taste of success, and now they're on the point of retiring from the game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retire' suggests leaving work, but here it means going to bed; the dash splits the wordplay into a success followed by the clipped word with 'they' wrapped around it.
explanation.definitionFit: Retiring for the night means going to bed, and hitting the hay is an informal idiom for exactly that.

clue.text: Rough for one to wear one? Right

definitions.text: Rough for one to wear one? Right

indicators.note: what is worn is put on around the wearer, so one piece encloses another

blocks.note: rough and harsh are synonyms
the Roman numeral for one, worn inside the previous word
again the Roman numeral
RT is a standard abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether such a scratchy garment is too harsh to put on, and is told yes.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue doubles as the definition: penitents wore this coarse garment precisely because it was rough on the skin.
explanation.definitionFit: A coarse goat-hair garment worn next to the skin as penance, uncomfortable by design, so rough for anyone wearing it.

clue.text: After function, leave for dance

blocks.note: tan is short for tangent, a trigonometric function
to leave is to go

explanation.surface: After a party or function, people head off to go dancing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Function' reads as a social event, but it is the mathematical sense; 'After' places the second piece after the first.
explanation.definitionFit: The Argentine ballroom routine for couples is one example of the general category of dances.

clue.text: Unusual thing to have bloke close to union at?

definitions.text: Unusual thing to have bloke close to union at?

indicators.note: something unusual is out of its normal form, so the letters are rearranged
the close of a word is its end, so only its final letter is used

blocks.note: a male, he
the closing letter of the word
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: It would be odd for a man to turn up at this pre-wedding celebration.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is also the definition: a bride's party before the wedding (the union) is women only, so a bloke there is unusual.
explanation.definitionFit: A British pre-wedding party for the bride and her female friends, held shortly before the marriage, where men are traditionally excluded.

clue.text: Rash — with smell — concealing a strange mark

indicators.note: to conceal is to hide inside, so one piece is enclosed by another

blocks.note: hum is British slang for a bad smell
taken as written
rum is British slang for odd
a scar is a mark on the skin

explanation.surface: A skin rash that smells and hides some odd mark: a doctor's nightmare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rash' looks like a skin complaint but is the adjective meaning reckless. In British slang, a hum is a stink and rum means odd.
explanation.definitionFit: Both describe a reckless, impetuous person who acts without thinking; the rhyming compound is a synonym for that adjective.

clue.text: He’s French, or would be indeed, if not very

indicators.note: the answer would become the other word if a letter were taken out, so that letter sits inside it

blocks.note: yes, indeed: an emphatic agreement
V is the abbreviation for very

explanation.surface: A Frenchman, or so he would be, unless the emphasis were removed.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing V from the name leaves YES, which means indeed; so the name is YES with V placed inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A common male first name in France, as in Yves Saint Laurent or Yves Montand, so it names a Frenchman.

clue.text: End of camping? Love to stop at home!

indicators.note: a stopper sits inside an opening, so one piece is plugged into another

blocks.note: camping means being in a tent
someone at home is in
love is zero in tennis, shaped like O

explanation.surface: A camper, at the end of a holiday, is just glad to be back home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'End of camping' looks like the last letter of camping; in fact 'End' alone is the definition, meaning aim.
explanation.definitionFit: An end can mean an aim or purpose, as in 'to that end', which is a synonym for one's plan.

clue.text: Tend to back employees running shows

indicators.note: the words display the letters, which are there in plain view inside them
going back means reading from right to left

blocks.note: the letters across the join of the two words, read back to front

explanation.surface: Managers usually back the staff who put on the shows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tend to back' reads as 'be inclined to support'; actually 'Tend to' is the definition and 'back' is the reversal signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To tend to a patient is to care for them, which is the verb meaning look after the sick.

clue.text: Taking off: one’s mass movement in art

blocks.note: taking off someone is mimicking them, doing an impression
one is I, so one's is I'S
M is the symbol for mass

explanation.surface: An art movement takes off, with mass participation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taking off' suggests a launch or success; here it is the British sense of mimicking someone.
explanation.definitionFit: The French painting school of Monet and Renoir, capturing light and fleeting moments, is a famous art movement.

clue.text: The end perhaps of Turkey’s objections recounted by ministers

indicators.note: to recount is to tell out loud, so the words are judged by how they sound

blocks.note: parsons are ministers of the church
noes are votes or objections against

explanation.surface: A diplomatic report on Turkey's final objections, as told by its ministers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turkey' looks like the country but is the bird; 'parsons' noes', the clergy's objections, is the spoken phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: The fatty rump at the tail end of a cooked bird, so the end of a turkey, hence 'perhaps' since chickens have one too.

clue.text: Men raised Deutschmarks in tax: something for a rainy day?

indicators.note: in a down clue, raising letters means reading them upwards, from bottom to top
placed in means put inside, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: to tax is to strain, put under pressure
OR is other ranks, soldiers who are not officers
DM is the abbreviation for the old German currency

explanation.surface: German money kept by men as tax savings, put aside for hard times.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For a rainy day' usually means savings, which the money and tax encourage; here it is literal, about rain. OR is other ranks in the army.
explanation.definitionFit: A grating and pipe that carries off water after heavy rain, so it is literally something used on wet days.

clue.text: Monarch no longer to block vote against old tyrant

indicators.note: a blockage sits inside a passage, so one piece goes into the middle of another

blocks.note: a vote against is a no
ER, Elizabeth Regina, the late queen

explanation.surface: A deposed king tries to obstruct a vote opposing some despot.
explanation.walkthrough: ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the crossword queen; 'no longer' fits since she has died.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman emperor notorious for cruelty, said to have fiddled while Rome burned, is a byword for an ancient despot.

clue.text: Make early sporting exit, but not be “distressed”

blocks.note: in golf, failing to qualify for the final rounds of a tournament
read as dis-tressed, losing one's tresses: not getting a haircut

explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks ask you to read 'distressed' as dis-tressed, deprived of tresses, so a trim; avoiding one is the second sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Golfers who score too poorly halfway through a tournament are eliminated, and someone skipping a haircut literally avoids being trimmed.

clue.text: Go out more? Missing Yankee’s not spotted

indicators.note: something missing has gone, so a letter is taken away

blocks.note: going out more means staying in less
Y is Yankee in the NATO alphabet; it is the letter removed

explanation.surface: Someone urged to get out more, while an absent American goes unseen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go out more?' is a phrase for its opposite, 'stay in less', written as one run of letters before the Y goes.
explanation.definitionFit: Something without stains has no spots or marks on it, so the word is a synonym for unblemished.

clue.text: One’s not sincere, on reflection, in thanks for snack

indicators.note: a reflection in a mirror shows things back to front
put in means placed inside, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: TX is a texting abbreviation for thanks
one is I, so one's is I'M
a liar is someone not sincere

explanation.surface: A guest, thinking it over, admits their thanks for the snack were insincere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One's' expands to 'I am', and the whole confession is reversed as a unit before being placed inside the texting shorthand for thanks.
explanation.definitionFit: A mixture of nuts, dried fruit and seeds eaten by hikers on the move, a classic portable snack.

clue.text: “Ta God” is, er a translation?

indicators.note: translating carries something into a new form, so these letters are moved into another order

blocks.note: the letters of these words, rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone hesitantly wonders whether 'Ta God' renders a Latin phrase.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the definition and the wordplay: 'ta' is British for thanks, so 'Ta God' is indeed a loose rendering of the Latin.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin liturgical phrase means 'thanks be to God', and 'ta' is informal British for thanks, so 'Ta God' paraphrases it.

clue.text: Book with education essentials? It’s fresh!

blocks.note: B is the abbreviation for book
the three Rs: reading, writing and arithmetic

explanation.surface: A new textbook covering the basics of schooling is hailed as innovative.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fresh' suggests new, but it is the weather sense: chilly. The three Rs are the basic school skills.
explanation.definitionFit: The shivering exclamation people make in cold weather, and a fresh day is a cool, breezy one.

clue.text: Area quiet after 5-hour party

indicators.note: coming after means placed later, so the pair of letters for the place and the hush go at the end

blocks.note: the answer to 5 Down is the NATO alphabet word for T
HR is the abbreviation for hour
A is the abbreviation for area
sh is a call for quiet

explanation.surface: A neighbourhood falls silent after a five-hour party.
explanation.walkthrough: '5-hour' points to the answer of 5 Down, TANGO, which is T in the NATO alphabet; 'after' puts the area-quiet pair at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Thrash is British slang for a lively party or celebration, as in a big birthday bash.

clue.text: One refusing to change out of uniform into elaborate stitched mink

indicators.note: going into something means entering it, so one letter is placed among others
to elaborate is to work something up into a more intricate form, so the letters are reworked

blocks.note: U is uniform in the NATO alphabet
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A soldier won't swap uniform for a fancy hand-stitched mink coat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Change out of uniform' reads as getting undressed; the definition stops at 'change', and 'out of' means made from.
explanation.definitionFit: An old-fashioned, conservative person who resists new ideas is idiomatically described as stuck and unwilling to move.

clue.text: One addressing autumn ending of off-peak fare

indicators.note: an ending is the final part, so only the last letter is taken

blocks.note: the final letter of the hyphenated word
fare as in food, eats

explanation.surface: A railway announcement about autumn timetables and cheaper off-peak tickets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fare' looks like a train ticket price but means food; 'addressing' is the poet's direct address in his ode.
explanation.definitionFit: The Romantic poet wrote 'To Autumn', an ode speaking directly to the season, so he addressed autumn.

clue.text: Each smartphone download potentially interrupted by ring

indicators.note: an interruption breaks into the middle, so one piece is put inside another

blocks.note: an application one might download to a phone
O is ring-shaped

explanation.surface: Every phone download gets cut off by an incoming call.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ring' suggests a phone call but is the letter O; 'potentially' marks the app as just one kind of download.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal phrase meaning per item, as in 'a pound a pop', so it is a colloquial synonym.

clue.text: Are Wanderers after quiet sort of tournament?

indicators.note: coming after means placed later, so the wandering piece goes second

blocks.note: P is piano, the musical direction for quiet
to be wanderers is to roam

explanation.surface: A football fan asks whether Wanderers, a club name, are going for a low-key competition.
explanation.walkthrough: Wanderers looks like a football club (Bolton or Wolves); read literally, 'are wanderers' means roam.
explanation.definitionFit: A golf competition pairing professionals with amateurs, so it is a particular type of event.

clue.text: Female porter maybe cross with artist

blocks.note: porter is a dark beer, an example of ale
a cross is shaped like X
with and and both join things
RA is a Royal Academician

explanation.surface: A woman hotel porter, perhaps irritated with a painter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Porter' suggests a doorman, but it is the beer; RA is a member of the Royal Academy of Arts.
explanation.definitionFit: A girl's name, given only to women, so it can be clued by the word for a woman.

clue.text: For silly short film turned to Sky

definitions.note: an adjective-looking word defining a noun, fair because 'silly' is also used as a noun for a foolish person, as in 'you big silly'

indicators.note: cut short means losing the end
in a down clue, turning skywards means reading from the bottom upwards

blocks.note: a recorded film; the end is dropped

explanation.surface: A goofy little clip is passed to the Sky TV network.
explanation.walkthrough: Sky is the British satellite TV company, but here it is the direction up. Div is British slang for an idiot.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang a div is a fool, which is what calling someone a silly means.

clue.text: Is earlier pressure one exerts moving Society?

indicators.note: things moving change position, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: P is the symbol for pressure
the Roman numeral for one
taken as written
S is the abbreviation for society

explanation.surface: Someone asks if an earlier campaign pressure is shifting society.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is earlier' looks like the start of a question, but it is the definition, a verb phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: To exist before something else is to come first in time, which is what being earlier means.

clue.text: Lack, for the most part, somewhere peaceful

indicators.note: most but not all of it is kept, so the tail is lost

blocks.note: to lack is to have not, written as one run of letters; the final two go

explanation.surface: A tranquil spot is mostly characterised by its lack of things.
explanation.walkthrough: Lack is a verb here: to lack is to 'have not', written as one run of letters with the last two dropped.
explanation.definitionFit: A harbour or place of safety and refuge, which is a calm, sheltered spot.
